sources.title: Queen's Gambit Declined: Complete Guide for Black (search snippet only; page returned 403)

overview: Black meets 2.c4 with 2...e6, holding d5 and keeping a secure, compact centre rather than taking the pawn. It is one of Black's most reliable defences to 1.d4 (s1). The price is the light-squared bishop on c8, which is shut in behind the e6-pawn and is Black's main strategic problem (s1). The game then usually becomes a manoeuvring fight: White uses the minority attack (b4-b5) in Carlsbad structures or central expansion with e4 or e4-e5 (Botvinnik plan), while Black aims for the freeing ...c5 or ...e5 break, a Lasker-style exchange of pieces, or a bishop fianchetto (s1, s2, s3). Both Wikipedia and Chessable stress that it is extremely sound yet can turn double-edged when both sides pursue their plans (s2). It was the staple of the Alekhine-Capablanca match (s1) and is played from beginner level to world champions (s2).

white_ideas.idea: Minority attack: b4-b5 against the Carlsbad structure to create a weak c6-pawn
Central break e3-e4, usually supported by f3 (and the Botvinnik plan e4-e5 to dislodge kingside defenders)
Kingsbury attack: Ne5 supported by f4 for a kingside assault
Exploit the passive c8-bishop, pin Nf6 with Bg5 in the traditional 4.Bg5 lines

black_ideas.idea: Liberating pawn break ...c5 (or ...e5), accepting isolated or hanging pawns for activity
Solve the c8-bishop problem: ...b6/...Bb7 fianchetto, Lasker's ...Ne4 exchanging pieces, or Ragozin ...Bb4
Queenside counterplay with ...a5 and ...b5 against White's plans
Time the ...c5 break carefully because exchanges can leave Black with an isolated pawn; piece activity matters

typical_structures.structure: Carlsbad: White c3/d4 vs Black c6/d5 after cxd5 exd5; White's minority attack against Black's queenside majority
Pawn tension on c4/d5 kept in the Orthodox lines, with the centre closed until a pawn break
Isolated queen's pawn or hanging pawns after Black's ...c5 break

character.notes: Described as a fundamentally solid, defensive approach and one of Black's most reliable defences to 1.d4 (s1). Chessable calls it 'extremely sound' with possibilities for both sides (s2). The play is strategic: the minority attack, central breaks and manoeuvring around the c8-bishop dominate, with fewer early forcing lines than in the Slav or Semi-Slav. Chess.com's taxonomy anchor treats the QGD Orthodox as Solid.

gambit.notes: Black declines, so no material changes hands. The name is historical; the taxonomy states the Queen's Gambit is not a gambit.

soundness.notes: Regarded as one of the most reliable defences for Black, played at championship level for a century (s1). No source suggests any dubious line in the main variations.

structure.notes: The centre stays tense or closed. The Carlsbad structure is called semi-closed (s3), with the d5 pawn held and the central break (e4 or ...c5) deferred. The typical middlegame has White's c4/d4 and Black's d5/e6 pawns in contact, exchanges coming later.

approach.notes: A main-line defence with a wide range of replies, not a universal system. Played at the highest level since Capablanca. Standard.

level.notes: Chessable says it suits players from beginner to World Champion and that the theory load is moderate; plans matter more than memorisation (s2). Black must still learn the ...c5 timing and how to free the c8-bishop. The side that studies it is Black. Intermediate fits.

sublines_that_differ.name: Exchange Variation (Carlsbad)
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. cxd5 exd5
sublines_that_differ.how: Symmetrical, minority attack vs kingside play; slower and more positional

sublines_that_differ.name: Tartakower / Lasker / Cambridge Springs
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Bg5
sublines_that_differ.how: Traditional 4.Bg5 lines; Cambridge Springs has tactical traps

sublines_that_differ.name: Ragozin
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Nf3 Bb4
sublines_that_differ.how: Pins the knight rather than ...Be7; active, between QGD and Nimzo

sublines_that_differ.name: Semi-Slav (via 3.Nf3 c6)
sublines_that_differ.how: Reaches the Semi-Slav; much sharper than QGD main lines (Botvinnik, Meran) (own understanding, unsourced)

sublines_that_differ.name: Tarrasch Defence
sublines_that_differ.how: Isolated queen's pawn; open and dynamic (own understanding, unsourced)

description.claim: A classical and robust defence, considered one of the most reliable responses to 1.d4
description.note: Wikipedia: one of Black's most reliable defences to 1.d4.

description.claim: It aims to create a solid central pawn structure
description.note: d5 and e6 give a secure foothold.

description.claim: It leads to a strategically rich game where long-term planning takes precedence over immediate tactical skirmishes
description.note: Strategic plans such as the minority attack dominate, though the opening can become double-edged.

description.claim: Ideal for patient players who understand pawn breaks, manoeuvring and small lasting advantages

common_plans.claim: For White: execute the minority attack (b4-b5) to create a weakness on c6, or use a space advantage
common_plans.note: Applies in the Carlsbad structure from the Exchange, not every QGD line.

common_plans.claim: For Black: a liberating break, typically ...c5 or ...e5
common_plans.note: Both are named as liberating breaks.

common_plans.claim: For Black: solve the problem of the light-squared bishop via fianchetto (...b6, ...Bb7), the Lasker manoeuvre (...Ne4) or the Ragozin set-up (...Bb4)
common_plans.note: Fianchetto, Lasker and the Ragozin are all QGD ways of dealing with the c8-bishop. Ragozin's ...Bb4 is more about activity than the bishop (own understanding).

common_plans.claim: Both sides often enter the Carlsbad pawn structure, where White plays on the queenside and Black seeks counterplay on the kingside or in the centre
common_plans.note: Carlsbad arises after cxd5 exd5; Black's play there is usually kingside or central, though Chessable also lists queenside ...a5/...b5 counterplay.
